A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MoSE research, with matching authors, core definitions and experiments. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original MoSE experiments on ZINC, QM9 and synthetic fractional-domination prediction, including additional results in Appendix B.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds evaluations on PCQM4Mv2-subset, CIFAR10, MNIST and peptide benchmarks, alongside new analyses in Appendix B.

M1.justification: The MoSE definition in Equation (1), motif and weighting parameterization, and replacement of GRIT's RRWP encodings with node-level MoSE remain unchanged. Additional motif configurations and the unrooted-homomorphism control expand evaluation of the existing framework.

E1.justification: V2 adds PCQM4Mv2-subset molecular regression, CIFAR10 and MNIST superpixel-graph classification, and Peptides-func/Peptides-struct classification and regression. These substantially extend coverage beyond v1's small-molecule and synthetic tasks to image-derived graphs and larger peptide molecules (Section 5.1; Appendices B.4–B.6).

E2.justification: The main encoding comparator set is retained. Local additions include MLP-E+Hom as a graph-level homomorphism comparator on QM9 (v2 Table 16) and new MNIST reference methods such as GAT and EGT (Table 8). The ZINC state-of-the-art comparison also replaces its GT entry with GT-E, already evaluated elsewhere in v1.

E3.justification: Reported settings change substantially: ZINC MLP-E moves from 4 to 8 layers and from 1,000 to 1,200 epochs, with numerous other configuration and search-range revisions (v1 Table 7; v2 Table 14). The retained QM9 transformer results are now described as GT without edge features, with 700 final epochs, versus GT-E with edge features and 1,200 epochs in v1. New benchmarks introduce additional budgets, metrics and protocols. These are documented setting revisions; unchanged result values do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: V2 adds motif-family and model-size sensitivity comparisons on CIFAR10 and MNIST (Tables 7 and 9), a node-rooted versus graph-level homomorphism comparison on QM9 (Table 16), and encoding computation-time analysis (Appendix B.1). The combined-encoding and ZINC edge-feature analyses already present in v1 are retained.

E5.justification: V2 explicitly identifies uncertainty as standard deviation and newly specifies four seeds for the retained synthetic experiment. V1 describes supplementary QM9 results as five-run averages; v2 distinguishes five runs for main-table GPS results from three runs for other appendix results (Appendix B.8). This revises run-count documentation without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial benchmark, sensitivity, control and timing results, including GPS+MoSE's 0.1133 MAE on PCQM4Mv2-subset and 73.50 accuracy on CIFAR10 (Table 1). The ZINC architecture comparison replaces GPS+RWSE's 0.070±0.002 with 0.069±0.001 under the separately described tuning protocol. QM9 appendix entries are corrected, including GPS+MoSE's mu value from 1.47 to 1.43. The headline GRIT+MoSE and main QM9 results remain unchanged; synthetic percentage-to-decimal conversion is equivalent rounding.

T1.justification: Proposition 4.2 gains the necessary non-isomorphic-graphs assumption. Appendix A.1 introduces explicit C1/C2 conventions for the RWSE correspondence, while Appendix B.1 adds treewidth-dependent complexity statements. The central expressivity theorems and most proofs remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the state-of-the-art claim from molecular prediction datasets in the plural to one dataset, consistent with the ZINC claim. The introduction consolidates its empirical contributions, while retaining the same central MoSE proposal and expressivity claims.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies v1's broad QM9 superiority statement by acknowledging GT exceptions on U0, U and H (Appendix B.8.1). It adds a redundancy/model-width explanation for mixed combined-encoding results, discusses computational costs and motif treewidth, and strengthens its interpretation of GRIT's performance without RRWP. The principal scientific interpretation remains intact.

D1.justification: Appendix B substantially expands reproducibility information with shared encoding and prediction-head details, optimizer and scheduler settings, warmup, dropout, explicit search procedures, and per-target QM9 configurations (Tables 18–21). It also documents new dataset splits and computation times. The hardware description and code link are retained.

R1.justification: Related work adds Chen et al. (2019) on function approximation and Maehara and NT (2024) on homomorphism networks. References expand for new datasets and complexity analysis, and the virtual-node discussion switches from Tönshoff et al. (2024) to Southern et al. (2025). The central positioning relative to homomorphism counting and Graph Transformers is unchanged.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized into cross-dataset encoding comparisons followed by separate architecture and RRWP comparisons on ZINC. Appendix B is rebuilt around shared protocols and detailed dataset/model subsections. Contribution statements and experimental explanations are extensively rewritten, although the theoretical exposition largely retains its structure.

P2.justification: Table 1 becomes a multi-dataset comparison with a PE/SE column, and the ZINC tables are rearranged. V1's synthetic bar chart and appendix results table are replaced by a main-text numerical table. V2 adds runtime, sensitivity, benchmark and configuration tables, and introduces ranking colors in retained appendix tables.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for applicability beyond small molecules through image and peptide benchmarks, and addresses v1's limited computational-cost and reproducibility documentation through Appendix B. Corrected theorem assumptions and QM9 entries further improve precision. Some ambiguities remain, including conflicting PCQM4Mv2 motif descriptions in Section 5.1 and Table 6, but the broader validation and more inspectable experimental procedures provide a clear overall quality improvement.
